claims.text: A CoCrFeMnNi-type high-entropy alloy can serve as an initially single-phase, compositionally homogeneous matrix for the proposed comparison.
Brittle behavior in initially single-phase high-entropy alloys emerges from thermal-history-induced changes in grain-boundary chemistry rather than from coarse conventional precipitates.
Prolonged moderate-temperature annealing promotes localized solute segregation at grain boundaries.
Prolonged moderate-temperature annealing promotes transient nanoscale precipitation at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary segregation and nanoscale precipitation reduce boundary cohesion and promote intergranular fracture.
Grain-boundary microstructure can govern intergranular ductility loss in a high-entropy alloy.
Brittleness can occur without formation of large classical precipitates.
Short-term high-temperature annealing minimizes grain-boundary segregation and transient precipitation.
Short-term high-temperature annealing preserves a comparatively uniform grain-boundary chemistry and higher ductility.
Prolonged moderate-temperature annealing will lower fracture toughness relative to short-term high-temperature annealing.
Prolonged moderate-temperature annealing will increase intergranular cracking relative to short-term high-temperature annealing.
Prolonged moderate-temperature annealing will reduce tensile ductility relative to short-term high-temperature annealing.
Minimal thermal exposure or inhibition of grain-boundary diffusion produces a ductile reference state with uniformly distributed solutes.
The proposed mechanism operates when moderate-temperature service exposure is long enough to permit significant grain-boundary diffusion.
The proposed mechanism is less significant during high-strain-rate loading or short-duration thermal exposure because diffusion is limited.
Single-phase high-entropy alloys can combine room-temperature ductility with high-temperature strength.
APT and TEM can be used in the proposed experiment to test for grain-boundary segregation and nanoscale precipitates.
